LESSON 1
AN INTRODUCTION TO THE EPISTLE OF JUDE
Scripture Text: Jude 1-2

The Epistle of Jude has been placed in the New Testament as a gateway to The Revelation. It is richer in symbolic language than any other book in the New Testament with the exception of The Revelation. The Acts of the Apostles clearly shows the acts of the “Apostles,” but the Epistle of Jude reveals the acts of the “apostates.” In this evening time of the Gospel Day, we are again facing the forces of apostasy. Jude has provided us with insight and revelation concerning the spirits that are promoting apostasy, the behavior that it produces, and how the enemy intends to work through apostasy today.
MEMORY VERSE: Is there any thing whereof it may be said, See, this is new? it hath been already of old time, which was before us (Ecclesiastes 1:10).
Jude, the Author

Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James. In the original Greek, the name Jude is actually Judas. The very title of this book brings to mind the person who will stand forever known as the world’s best example of the worst apostate–Judas Iscariot! In the New Testament, five notable men were called Judas, but this man is clearly identified as the brother of James. James was the pastor of the Jerusalem congregation, the author of the Epistle of James, and one of the four brothers of the Lord (Matthew 13:55).
Preventions of Apostasy

Attributes portrayed by both Jude and James can prevent one’s being infected with apostasy. One attribute is humility. Notice, Jude did not mention the fact that he was the Lord’s brother. This shows the lack of carnal pride. Proverbs 13:10 states, “Only by pride cometh contention.” Unfeigned humility causes one “not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think” (Romans 12:3).

Another attribute is servitude. Both Jude and James stated that they were servants. The English word servant is the word doulos in the original Greek and means much more than a servant. It means “a slave,” or literally, “a bondslave.”

The greatest prevention of our apostatizing or backsliding is to be continually aware that we are the Church of God. We have been purchased with Jesus Christ’s blood (Acts 20:28). We should glorify God in our bodies and in our spirits, which are God’s. One who is truly a slave to the Master and His Word will never apostatize.
The Audience Addressed by Jude

To them that are sanctified by God the Father, and preserved in Jesus Christ, and called. The word called is derived from the Greek word kalein, which means “the summoning of a man to office, to duty, and to responsibility.” It represents the saints’ call to arms. They are to be watchful for the most subtle moves of the enemy. The word sanctified comes from the Greek word hagiazo and means “the setting apart of the believer for God.” We must be set apart and totally yielded to God with self kept under to maintain victory over apostasy.

The word preserved comes from a Greek word that means “kept,” or “continually kept.” It expresses watchful care and close attention. The Apostle Paul referred to his readers as sanctified and called, but Jude added preserved to show, right in verse one, that no matter how great the opposing force may be, Christ has made provision for His people to be “continually kept.”

LESSON 1
Mercy, Peace, and Love

Mercy unto you, and peace, and love, be multiplied. This second verse is more than a courteous salutation; it is the only such statement in the entire Bible. The Apostle Paul used the phrase “grace be unto you, and peace” in Colossians 1:2, but Jude used the word Mercy, meaning “an outward manifestation of pity.” It assumes there is a need on the part of the person who receives it and reveals describes man’s upward look to God. Peace depicts man’s inward look at what God gives. Love radiates from man’s heart through his outward look. These verses describe the qualities the church needs to maintain constant victory in these troublesome times.
JUST A THOUGHT

LESSON 2
JUDE’S BURDEN
Scripture Text: Jude 3

This lesson reveals the burden behind Jude’s letter. Jude was in the process of drafting a doctrinal treatise but set it hastily aside when necessity and inspiration prompted him, because his divinely inspired burden compelled him to write. In our day, when many make a professional vocation out of religion, the true church still looks for those who have been divinely called and have a burden prompting them in what they do.
MEMORY VERSE: For though I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of: for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:16)!
Letter to the Church

Beloved. Jude addressed his readers as Beloved. He was speaking to those whom God loves, those who have been born again. They are the ones who can understand spiritual truth. 1 Corinthians 2:14 reads, “But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.”

The Greek word for beloved is agapetos. It is derived from another Greek word, agapao, which stands for divine love, a never changing love. Jude wrote this letter to the church–a people whose true love for Christ and truth is unchanging, even in changing times.
The Common Salvation

When I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation. Another translation of this phrase reads, “When I was in the midst of devoting all my energy to writing to you about the faith we all share.” Both phrases teach that we will each have the same salvation: it will work in the same manner in all.

The word common comes from the Greek word koinos and means “shared by all.” Concerning doctrinal truths and standards, the common salvation will not lead some people in one direction and others in a contrary direction. If that is occurring, something other than real salvation is working. Ones may claim it is salvation, but if it is not common, it is not real.
Unchangeable Word of Truth

Exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints. Jude wrote this epistle in A.D. 66, only thirty-three years after the Day of Pentecost. His real reason for writing was to reveal that an apostasy was already under way. That which was being presented to the people as salvation and Christianity was not really the faith but a cleverly disguised counterfeit.

The words contend for the faith . . . once delivered unto the saints hold several truths. One, the faith is delivered. Truth is not some “vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers” (1 Peter 1:18). It is not something that comes by education but by revelation. Peter spoke concerning prophecy, but this principle is true of all Scriptures: “Holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2 Peter 1:21). The Apostle Paul said, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2 Timothy 3:16).

Malachi 3:6 says, “For I am the L ORD , I change not.” Since the Source of Truth is unchanging and settled, so is His truth. Psalm 119:89 states, “Forever, O L ORD , thy word is settled in heaven.” The faith is still what mankind needs today.

Three, truths was given to saints. Notice, the word is saints (plural). Truth is not the possession of any one individual: it comes down within the church, it is understood by the church, and the church is responsible to propagate it.

Four, truth must be defended. In the text, the word contend actually means “to defend.” Bagster’s Greek Lexicon says this word means “to contend strenuously in defense of.” The word Jude used contains the root of our English word agony. Defending the Word, or the truth, may not always be easy or comfortable: it may cause some agony. In this day of ease, many do not want to be inconvenienced, but in order to preserve the truth and defend the faith, we may suffer much discomfort. However, it is better to be uncomfortable here for a season than for all eternity.

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 3
EARMARKS OF APOSTATES
Scripture Text: Jude 4

In this lesson, Jude exposed the earmarks of the apostate elements that were working. This epistle and others have been preserved down through the years to help us understand these conditions when we see them developing. Jude has shown us that the only way to deal with apostasy is with truth. Truth is plain and pointed; it exposes wrong.

Ephesians 6:12 says, “For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness [or wicked spirits] in high places [another text says „heavenlies‟].” In today‟s society when one raises his voice against wrong or apostasy, he is quickly branded as having a bad spirit. In the light of our text, the one who promotes a teaching, a doctrine, or a stance contrary to the sound teaching of the Scriptures is the one with a bad spirit.

MEMORY VERSE: For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world (Titus 2:11-12).
Workers of Deceit

There are certain men crept in unawares. Here is the peril that prompted Jude to write this flaming epistle. Why such alarm? The danger to the church was coming from within! Men who were not actually in the church– the body of Christ–were being accepted as brethren in the congregation, making their influence and teachings dangerous.

In the original Greek language, the word pareisduein is used for the words crept in unawares. It describes the slow and subtle entry of new ways or ideas that seek to undermine and break down traditional values. It always indicates something evil coming into a society or a situation. This word represents a clever pleader who–by his logic, his argument, and his persuasive personality–wins the minds of a judge and jury. It is also used to portray an outlaw slipping back into a country from which he had been deported. Jude 4 in The Amplified Bible reads, “For certain men have crept in stealthily [gaining entrance secretly by a side door].” John 10:1 states, “He that entereth not by the door [Jesus] . . . the same is a thief and a robber.”

Jesus spoke of apostasy in Matthew 13:25 when he said, “But while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat.” The enemy‟s introduction of deceitful men into the Christian community was as disastrous as tares being sown into a crop of wheat. Tares entwine their roots around wheat and when they are removed, the wheat is ripped up as well. This is how deadly it can be when people like that work in a congregation if the “wheat” is not truly “rooted and grounded” (Ephesians 3:17). Matthew 15:13 says, “Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up.” So, the first earmark of apostates is that these people work slowly and undercover. If they were dealing truthfully, they would not have to work in such an underhanded manner.
Perverting God’s Grace

Ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness. The second earmark of a move made by an apostate is that it leans toward less godliness. It lowers the standard of holiness and makes provision for the flesh. This is always a sure indicator of apostasy!

Apostates do not outwardly appear to be ungodly men (this is a general term that includes women as well). This term is derived from the Greek word abebes, which means “one destitute of reverential awe toward God.” The reason these ones can accomplish such a deceptive work is that they do not tremble at God‟s Word! Jesus

said they are “like unto whited sepulchres” that “outwardly appear righteous unto men” (Matthew 23:27-28).

Concerning externals, these people are blameless, but “within they are full of extortion and excess” (verse 25). The Amplified Bible is more graphic: “Within they are full of extortion (prey, spoil, plunder) and grasping self-indulgence.”

The men who lacked the fear of God in Jude‟s day took hold of that which was divine and began to alter it, over a period of time, to suit their own fleshly purposes. Through persistence, they began turning the grace (the strength, or power) of our God into lasciviousness (blatant immorality).

In the first century there were two groups of people known as the Antinomians and the Gnostics. These individuals embraced lawlessness. They taught that matter was wholly evil; therefore, the body being matter was evil–so man could not live holy–but the grace of God would cover any sin. This meant that man could sin as much as he wanted, because the more he sinned, the greater the grace. The Bible‟s response to such a teaching is, “Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid” (Romans 6:1-2).
Denying the Lord

Denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ. The third earmark of apostates is denial. When the thought of denying the only Lord God is raised, people think it means to actually deny that He exists, but this is not what the Scripture text implies. How do ones deny God? Titus 1:16 tells us that they profess to know Him; but really, in works they deny Him. The Amplified Bible says, “They profess to know God [to recognize, perceive and be acquainted with Him] but deny and disown and renounce Him by what they do.”

Christ is referred to as our Lord Jesus Christ. This phrase portrays the three offices of Christ. One, He is Sovereign of the universe and “Lord of all” (Acts 10:36). Two, He is Jesus, which means “Jehovah the Savior.” Three, He is Christ, or Christos, in Greek and Messiah in Hebrew, which means “The Anointed One,” the fulfillment of Old Testament prophecy.

The apostates in Jude‟s day denied Christ lordship of their lives, refused His salvation and deliverance, and discarded Him as “The Anointed One.” They denied Him in works and substituted another gospel for the truth (Galatians 1:6). However, God is faithful. He has had a ministry to sound forth an alarm in every age of time. Whether we heed it or not in our day will determine our outcome.
JUST A THOUGHT
Failure may be an event; it need not be a person.

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 4
ISRAEL AS A REMINDER
Scripture Text: Jude 5

In this Scripture, Jude has introduced illustrations to remind the saints of the terrible consequences that came upon ones in the past who did not believe. It is revealed to us that the Lord does not hold people responsible for what they have never seen or understood. The real danger to the saints is that after having known truth, walked in it, and testified to it, they might let it become a reality of the past. This is just how apostasy works. It moves people from the position they occupy in the truth to a totally different position, while all the time they think they have not moved. That is why God prompted Jude to bring up these Old Testament examples.
MEMORY VERSE: For if I build again the things which I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor. ─Galatians 2:18
Stirring Our Remembrance

I will therefore put you in remembrance. This phrase reveals three things. One, knowledge is necessary for there to be sin. James 4:17 tells us, “Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin.” Jesus said, “If ye were blind, ye should have no sin: but now ye say, We see; therefore your sin remaineth” (John 9:41).

Two, man is a forgetful creature. God ordained that we constantly be reminded by the ministry. 2 Peter 1:12-13 states: “Where-fore I will not be negligent to put you always in remembrance of these things, though ye know them, and be established in the present truth. Yea, I think it meet, as long as I am in this tabernacle, to stir you up by putting you in remembrance.”

Three, being repetitious is the evidence of a good minister (see 1 Timothy 4:6). We should never become weary with repetition, for just as it is in the military, repeated drills can mean the difference between life and death.
The Great Deception

Though ye once knew this. This statement is proof that apostasy had truly made an inroad in Jude’s day and was effective in its work even as it is today. Precious truths that were once carefully considered and lovingly guarded were being viewed as excessive or fanatical and looked upon with disdain and scorn. 2 Peter 2:22 describes it this way: “But it is happened unto them according to the true proverb, The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire.” A dog that returns to its own vomit partakes of what once made it sick.

Apostates build again what they once destroyed. They are people who have moved to a past-tense experience while making a present-tense profession, just as Saul did. Saul said, “Blessed be thou of the LORD: I have performed the commandment of the LORD” (1 Samuel 15:13). He thought he had obeyed. The truth was, he had disobeyed! This is the deception of apostasy.
Unbelief and Pride

How that the Lord, having saved the people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed them that believed not. Here Jude was confronting those who had been moved by apostasy with the sobering reminder of the Exodus account (see Numbers, Chapters 13-14). Israel was at the very borders of the Promised Land, at Kadish-Barnea. Twelve spies had been sent out to survey the land. Of the twelve, ten brought back an evil report

that caused the people to murmur against Moses and Aaron. God heard their words and saw their unbelief. He said, “Your carcasses shall fall in this wilderness” (Numbers 14:29). Of those who were twenty and older, only Joshua and Caleb made it into Canaan.

We must know one thing to understand this example: the men who were corrupting the church then did not regard themselves as enemies of the truth. They considered themselves to be advanced thinkers–a cut above the ordinary saints. They were, by their own estimation, the spiritual elite. Jude chose this example of old Israel to show that even if God has favored people with great privileges, they can still fall away into disaster. Consider those in the past: Adam, Samson, Saul, Solomon, Judas, and Demas. We must be on constant watch against that which could destroy us. New Testament Warnings

The remembrance of what happened to old Israel haunted the minds of the New Testament ministers, who were as responsible for leading God’s people as Moses was in the Exodus. The Israelites had been delivered miraculously, just as the people in our study of Jude were genuinely delivered out of sin, but later on they were destroyed. Why? Because of their unbelief. We must believe the report and obey the Gospel to stay saved. Those with the sense of a superior spirituality do not feel they need to believe. They are moved by spirits with teachings that are contrary to sound doctrine. This is why Paul said, “But with many of them God was not well pleased . . . . Now these things were our examples” (1 Corinthians 10:5-6).

Jude as well as Paul was trying to awaken those who were falling prey to the enemy so that they would not repeat the errors of the past. John Wesley warned, “Let none presume on past mercies, as if they were out of danger.” 1 Corinthians 10:12 warns, “Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.” There is no place of safe spiritual footing except the place of full obedience.
JUST A THOUGHT
It is a terrible thing to fall, but it is worse yet to fall and think you are still standing!

Here Jude was confronting those who had been moved by apostasy with the sobering reminder of the Exodus account (see Numbers, Chapters 13-14).
Israel was at the very borders of the Promised Land, at Kadish-Barnea.

They considered themselves to be advanced thinkers–a cut above the ordinary saints.
They were, by their own estimation, the spiritual elite.

We must be on constant watch against that which could destroy us.
New Testament Warnings
The remembrance of what happened to old Israel haunted the minds of the New Testament ministers, who were as responsible for leading God’s people as Moses was in the Exodus.
The Israelites had been delivered miraculously, just as the people in our study of Jude were genuinely delivered out of sin, but later on they were destroyed.
Why?
Because of their unbelief.
We must believe the report and obey the Gospel to stay saved.
Those with the sense of a superior spirituality do not feel they need to believe.
They are moved by spirits with teachings that are contrary to sound doctrine.
This is why Paul said, “But with many of them God was not well pleased . . . .
Now these things were our examples” (1 Corinthians 10:5-6).
Jude as well as Paul was trying to awaken those who were falling prey to the enemy so that they would not repeat the errors of the past.
John Wesley warned, “Let none presume on past mercies, as if they were out of danger.”
1 Corinthians 10:12 warns, “Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.”
There is no place of safe spiritual footing except the place of full obedience.
It is a terrible thing to fall, but it is worse yet to fall and think you are still standing!

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 5
THE FALLEN ANGELS
Scripture Text: Jude 6

This verse has generated much confusion in the religious realm. Some believe the word angels refers to celestial beings. They make reference to Genesis 6:2 and claim that this is where angelic beings fell away. Others say Jude 6 refers to the supposed revolt in Heaven, spoken of in Isaiah 14:12: “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer.” However, Isaiah 14:16 lets us know that Lucifer was a man, not an angelic being. If the word angels do not always represent celestial creatures, what angels did Jude mean then when he wrote verse 6?
MEMORY VERSE: I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called. ─Ephesians 4:1
The Nature of This Epistle

Many commentators believe verse 6 must have an Old Testament literal fulfillment since verse 5 speaks of old Israel and verse 7 speaks of Sodom and Gomorrah. However, it is necessary to understand the two-part teaching style of this epistle. It is known as parallelism. In verse 4, Jude wrote of men who fostered apostasy in his day, the first century. In verse 5, he used an example from the Old Testament. In verse 6, when he spoke of angels, he was again referring to ones in the first century.

Notice the pattern: starting again in verse 7 and continuing through verse 16, every other reference goes from the Old Testament example to the New Testament reality to show similarities or differences. In verse 6, he was dealing with the New Testament reality.
Are There Sinning Angels?

The angels which kept not their first estate. When Peter dealt with this same truth, he said, “God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell” (2 Peter 2:4). These words are confusing to people in false religion because they do not properly understand sin. There must be a power of choice to sin. James 4:17 says, “Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin.” The phrase “doeth it not” portrays a power of choice, and the Scriptures do not teach that heavenly angelic beings have the power of choice.

James 1:14 says that “every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.” Where does “lust,” or desire, come from? 1 John 2:16 tells us: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.” Before one can sin, there must be temptation. Temptation requires a fleshly, human nature. Celestial beings cannot be tempted to sin because they do not have human natures. Therefore, these angels were not celestial beings.

The Greek word for angels is aggelos. It means “a messenger, a minister, or a pastor.” Jesus said in Revelation 1:20, “The seven stars are the angels [aggelos] of the seven churches.” This text is dealing with ministers or pastors who became instruments of apostasy, not celestial beings.

Jude and Peter were both speaking of a ministry that was angelic in the sense that it had been exalted “in heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:6). However, something happened. They kept not their first estate. The Amplified Bible says that they “did not keep (care for, guard and hold to) their own first place of power but abandoned their proper dwelling place.” What was “their proper dwelling place”? Psalm 90:1 says, “L ORD , thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations.” They left their proper abode when they left the truth.

LESSON 5
A Fallen Ministry

Left their own habitation. When Jesus inspired the letter that represents the time period of A.D. 33-270, He said, “Thou hast left thy first love” (Revelation 2:4). How did those ministers leave their “first love”? According to Revelation 2:1-7, they were zealously practicing religion, but they had let it become a “form of godliness” (2 Timothy 3:5). They failed to keep their experiences clear and sinned by substituting “the commandments of men” for truth (Matthew 15:9).

When ones apostatize, they leave the church. The church is the “habitation of God through the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:22). When they continue to practice religion, they become part of spiritual Babylon, “the habitation of devils” (Revelation 18:2). They are then called “the angels that sinned” (2 Peter 2:4). If God did not spare Judas Iscariot, Demas, Hymenaeus, and Philetus, we need not think He will spare us from judgment if we deviate from truth. “God is no respecter of persons” (Acts 10:34).
Chains Unto Judgment

He hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day. These chains are not literal. They typify the binding spiritual state that men go into. John 12:35 says to “walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you.” Matthew 6:23 declares, “How great is that darkness!” There is no greater darkness than that which comes upon ones who have had light and refused to walk in it. This is why we should “walk as children of light” (Ephesians 5:8).
JUST A THOUGHT
If you are headed the wrong way, God allows U-turns.

LESSON 6
SODOM AND GOMORRAH
Scripture Text: Jude 7

This lesson focuses on the grim reminder of the final outcome of apostasy–the account of the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah (see Genesis, Chapter 19). It is used again and again in the Scriptures as the example of the sins of men and the judgment of God.

Following the teaching method of parallelism, Jude 7 deals with the historical reference, and verse 8 parallels that verse with reference to the time in which Jude was writing. As we consider this example, may God help us to realize that apostasy begins with intellectual doubts or a seemingly mild, spiritual deviance, but it is certain to end in physical degradation of some form.
MEMORY VERSE: Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death. ─James 1:15
From Truth to Apostasy

Even as Sodom and Gomorrah, and the cities about them in like manner. These two cities are mentioned in connection with apostasy because they once had a knowledge of truth. Ussher’s Chronology says that only 450 years had passed after the Flood when the destruction of these cities took place. Before that, God had let the king of Sodom be exposed to Abraham when he rescued Lot (see Genesis 14:8-24), who had been living in their midst as a “righteous man” (2 Peter 2:8). Shem, Noah’s son, died fifty-one years after the destruction of these cities. He would have been a vivid reminder of God’s character, His truth, and His judgment. The point is clear that before God brings judgment or vengeance, He first gives an opportunity for repentance. Great is God’s faithfulness! No one has ever truly apostatized without first having had truth.

Sodom and Gomorrah were not the only cities to be subjected to God’s outpouring of wrath. Jude said the cities about them suffered too. In all, four cities were destroyed (see Deuteronomy 29:23). This plainly shows that apostasy does not stay confined; it spreads just as a cancer does. What happened to those four cities shows us that this is how apostasy works.
The Sin of Sodom and Gomorrah

Giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh. In Genesis 19:5, the men of the city asked Lot, “Where are the men which came in to thee this night? bring them out . . . that we may know them.” Lot understood what was meant by the phrase “that we may know them.” He said, “I pray you, brethren, do not so wickedly” (verse 7). The word know is used other places in the Scriptures where its meaning is different, but here it means the same as in Genesis 4:1: “Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain.” Here, the words know and knew mean “in the most intimate fashion, in a sexual sense.”

Jude 7 mentions fornication (voluntary, intimate sexual behavior between ones not married) and strange flesh. What is strange flesh? Romans 1:27 explains it: “And likewise also the men, leaving the natural use of the woman, burned in their lust one toward another; men with men working that which is unseemly . . . .” This verse is speaking of the sin of homosexuality. We may not think there could be any connection between this type of activity and apostasy, but religious organizations of today–some of these organizations once had light that was brought forth by great reformers–are embracing this sin and ordaining homosexuals to be ministers.

These “ministers” are raising up congregations and even performing same-sex marriages. This shows that when apostasy starts in the minds and hearts of people, there is no limit to how low they may go. But as vile,

heinous, and repulsive as homosexuality is, was this the sin that really stirred God or was it merely the outgrowth of something worse? Romans 1:18 tells us that God’s wrath is stirred “against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness.” What was the “ungodliness and unrighteousness” that those men were committing? They were professing to have truth, but they had twisted it to sanction wrong. This always stirs God!

Romans 1:21-22 says that those men “knew God . . . but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened. Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools.” Verse 25 says they “changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator.” This is what was fatal! We must not let our humanity and our thinking cause us to start changing the truth, or we will end up with darkened hearts as they did.
A Supernatural Fire

Suffering the vengeance of eternal fire. There are two great revelations in this phrase. One, the inhabitants of these cities are still suffering. They are in eternal agony. Their suffering merely went from the realm of the seen to the unseen (even though we cannot see them, the realities of hell are still there). Two, this eternal fire came directly from God, and it was a combination of “brimstone and fire” (Genesis 19:24).

This gives us an understanding of the kind of fire that shall be on the Judgment Day. 2 Peter 3:12 says, “. . . the heavens being on fire shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat.” The fire that fell on Sodom and Gomorrah was an example of the supernatural fire that will melt natural fire on the Judgment Day. (This supernatural fire is so potent that after God had used it on those cities, they became the site where the Dead Sea is today.)

The fact we should learn from all of this is that the end of apostasy is a terrible death with far reaching, eternal consequences. This lesson should serve as a warning. When you see ones moving from truth, think of how far they might go and of how severe the judgment that awaits them will be. Be true and do not allow your imagination to move you in this day.
JUST A THOUGHT
No matter how spotted your past may be, your future is unspotted.

blocks.text: SUNDAY SCHOOL MATERIALS FOR ADULTS
LESSON 7
FILTHY DREAMERS
Scripture Text: Jude 8
In verse 8, Jude was speaking of his day, and he used the historical accounts in verses 7 and 9 in a parallel fashion to give us understanding of the outgrowths of the nature of apostasy.
MEMORY VERSE: But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil. ─Matthew 5:37
Vain Dreamers

Likewise also these filthy dreamers defile the flesh. By using the word likewise, or in like manner, Jude wanted his readers to think back to verses 4, 6, and 7. He wanted us to think of the sinful actions that were committed there and of the ones who were responsible for them. In the King James Version, Jude called these ones filthy dreamers. The actual Greek translation is “these dreaming ones.” Another translation says it this way: “These men, too, cherish vain dreams.” All these translations mean the same thing: apostasy starts with ones who cherish wrong dreams, or wrong thinking.

The word dream comes from the Greek word enupnion meaning “something seen in sleep.” Webster’s New World Dictionary tells us it means “thoughts passing through a sleeping person’s mind.” Vain dreams are not of a divine origin nor are they sound, and following them leads to defilement of the flesh. Any divinely inspired thought will lead to more spirituality not less. This truth proves that apostasy is a result of wrong thinking. This is why we should be “casting down imaginations, and . . . bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5). Unwholesome thoughts will enter our minds, so we do need to guard our thoughts. If they are allowed entrance to the heart, they will manifest themselves through the flesh.
Despisers of Church Government

Despise dominion. 2 Peter 2:10 also deals with the same thought of despising government. It says, “But chiefly them that walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness, and despise government. Presumptuous are they, self-willed, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities.” When Peter said that they “despise government,” he was not speaking of civil government. He meant church government. Both Jude and Peter taught that apostates will assault divinely instituted church government.

The word dominion comes from the Greek word kuriotes, which means “rulers, dominions, and governments.” The true church is not an anarchy. It is a theocracy; it is governed by divine rule. Ephesians 4:11 tells us that God gave some men the gifts of being apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers.

Hebrews 13:17 admonishes us to “obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves.” Who rules over us? The ministry. In Revelation 4:4 the ministry is called the “four and twenty elders,” an illusion to the Levitical priesthood. 1 Chronicles 24:5 says the ministry is “the governors of the sanctuary, and governors of the house of God.” 1 Timothy 3:15 states, “The house of God . . . is the church of the living God.”
Fearless Speakers

Speak evil of dignities. Peter said that apostates are “Pre-sumptuous” and “self-willed.” They want to yield to evil dreams and evil thoughts because they appeal to self and to an unrestrained will. Since apostates dislike to be governed by truth, they will attempt to change it to make it compatible with their self-will. Anything or

anyone that attempts to place any control or restraint on their flesh or carnal desires and activities is going to be an object of their scorn.

When apostates feel that someone is attempting to set forth divine government that will place restrictions on the flesh, they immediately attack by speaking against those who are honored and esteemed. In every age, those who have wanted to change the direction of the church have done this. Their purpose for discrediting the leaders is to turn the heads of the people. They are not afraid to speak evil of leaders because they have lost the fear of God, and they feel that they should be the leaders.
A Good Test

Can you see how self-will helps promote apostasy? Dreams or thoughts that are not brought into captivity, in obedience to Christ, go to the heart. Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.” Proverbs 23:7 states, “For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he.” In other words, what gets into your heart determines how you live.

A good test to put on any dream, thought, or doctrine when it comes to you is to ask yourself these questions: “What effect will this have on my overall spirituality? How victorious are the ones who are trying to persuade me?” Matthew 7:15 says, “Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing.” Jesus said to check the fruits of people’s lives because “by their fruits ye shall know them” (Matthew 7:20). See what a person’s life produces before you give any consideration to following that individual’s lifestyle.
JUST A THOUGHT
It is not the tracks before that throw us but the tracks that are behind us.

LESSON 8
MICHAEL THE ARCHANGEL
Scripture Text: Jude 9

In verse 9, Jude again reverted to another historical account to bring us understanding of his argument regarding those in verse 8 who “speak evil of dignities.” He brought up the interesting account concerning Michael the archangel and the dispute about the body of Moses to teach that, even in the face of opposition, there is a right way to behave.

MEMORY VERSE: For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps: Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth. ─1 Peter 2:21-22
One Who Is Like God

Michael. Who is this? The name Michael in the original Greek language as well as in the Hebrew language means “One who is like God.” Some translations say that it means “Who is like God?” Two references to the name Michael are in the Book of Daniel. In Daniel 10:21, it says, “Michael your prince,” and Daniel 12:1 says, “Michael . . . the great prince.” In each case Daniel refers to Michael as a “prince.” Who is this “One who is like God,” a “prince”?

In John 14:8 Philip said, “Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us,” Jesus’ reply in verse 9 was, “Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father.” Jesus stated in John 10:30, “I and my Father are one,” and Hebrews 1:3 declares that Christ is the brightness of God’s glory, “the express image [copy] of his person.”

Jesus Christ is the “One who is like God.” He is Michael. Since Jesus is Michael, He is also the “prince” in Daniel’s prophecy and in the Messianic prophecy in Isaiah 9:6, which says, “. . . the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called . . . The Prince of Peace.”
The Master of Angels

The archangel. While the name Michael is used in reference to Christ five times in the Scriptures, the word archangel is used only twice. It is always used in the singular form and is composed of two words: arch and angel. The word arch means “chief or master.” (It comes from the Greek word archo, which means “to be first in political rule or power.”) The word angel means “a messenger,” or one messenger. There is not a host of archangels since there can be only one chief, or master.

Who is the archangel? Matthew 26:53 asks the question, “Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels?” 1 Thessalonians 4:16 states, “For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God . . . .” If “the Lord himself” has “the voice of the archangel,” it only stands to reason that “the Lord himself” is the archangel. Religions that teach that Lucifer and Gabriel are archangels have no basis in truth. The word archangel is not used with any name in the Scriptures other than Michael, who is Jesus Christ.
Disputation With the Devil

Contending with the devil . . . about the body of Moses. It was necessary to establish the identity of the archangel because in Jude’s account, Michael the archangel contended with the devil . . . about the body of Moses. This contention was very familiar to first century Jewish converts. It is mentioned in The Targum of Jonathan, in Oecumenius, and in The Assumption of Moses. Briefly, they say that the Lord desired to hide Moses’ body so that the people of Israel would not be tempted to worship the leaders of the past. In the dispute,

The Amplified Bible reads, “The archangel Michael, contending with the devil . . . dared not [presume to] bring an abusive condemnation against him, but said, The Lord rebuke you!” Jude reasoned that if Jesus Christ, Michael the archangel, with His superior position, knowledge, and power, would not stoop to accuse the devil, then why should anyone else be so presumptuous and “speak evil of dignities” (verse 8)? Matthew 10:24 says, “The disciple is not above his master, nor the servant above his lord.”

LESSON 9
THE BRUTE BEASTS
Scripture Text: Jude 10

Jude has again changed the topic back to the time in which he was writing and used another term that has caused much confusion in religious organizations: the word beasts. In this lesson, we will identify who these beasts are, then many other Scriptures will become understandable as well.
MEMORY VERSE: And hereby we do know that we know him, if we keep his commandments. ─1 John 2:3
Blasphemous Words

But these speak evil. This phrase begins with the conjunction But, meaning the truths in this verse are connected with the previous verses, especially verses 4, 6, and 8. The “certain men [who] crept in unawares,” the “ungodly men,” the “angels which kept not their first estate,” and the “filthy dreamers” are the ones who speak evil. Jude was still dealing with the agents of apostasy; and a predominant characteristic of apostates is their talk.

When apostates speak evil, what does it actually mean? The Greek translation reads, “These blaspheme.” The Greek word used for speak evil is the same Greek word used in Revelation 13:6, in speaking of the beast that “opened his mouth in blasphemy against God, to blaspheme his name, and his tabernacle, and them that dwell in heaven.” Apostates speak blasphemy!
Why They Knew Not

Things which they know not. The word know implies more in Greek than in English. In English, it appears twice in verse 10, but in the Greek language two different words are used. In the phrase know not, the word know comes from the Greek word oida, meaning “a deeper knowledge, a divine knowledge.” Why did they know not? 1 Corinthians 2:14 says, “But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.”

Why is the speech of apostates considered so blasphemous? 2 Peter 2:12 parallels Jude 10: “But these, as natural brute beasts . . . speak evil of the things that they understand [or know] not.” Apostates “have forsaken the right way, and are gone astray” (2 Peter 2:15). Their evil words are much worse than those of unbelievers because they once had a divine revelation of truth and submitted to its authority, but now they know not.
Perception by the Senses

They know naturally. Throughout the Scriptures, the King James Version uses the word beasts. Paul said in 1 Corinthians 15:32, “I have fought with beasts at Ephesus.” The Revelation refers repeatedly to beasts. In Revelation 13:1, John saw “a beast rise up out of the sea.” In verse 11, he saw a “beast coming up out of the earth.” Were these hideous literal animals? No. What were the Scripture writers symbolizing then? This question brings us to the second time the word know is used in verse 10.

In the phrase know naturally, the word know comes from the Greek word epistad, which refers to perception by the animal faculties. Apostates lose all spiritual perception of truths they once had and can only understand what is revealed to their natural senses. The word naturally comes from the Greek word physikos, meaning “to be governed by mere natural instincts.” Together, the words know naturally give us a better understanding of

It means “irrational or unreasonable.” The Amplified Bible translates this part of verse 10 to read, “whatever they do understand physically . . . like irrational beasts.” The word beasts, in this verse, comes from the Greek word zoon, which is derived from the word zoe, meaning physical life. LESSON 10
THE WAY OF CAIN
Scripture Text: Jude 11

Verse 11 is really the heart of Jude’s letter. Apostasy in history is depicted in the verses before it, and apostasy in prophecy is shown in the verses following it. It is the only verse in the entire letter where Jude used more than one Old Testament illustration. In this text, Jude reminds us of three infamous Old Testament characters: Cain, Balaam, and Core. He is telling how these historical figures were like the apostates of his day. In this lesson, we want to study the first one: Cain.
MEMORY VERSE: Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come. ─1 Corinthians 10:11
The Power of Choice

Woe unto them! for they have gone. This verse begins with a sharp pronouncement upon those apostates described in the previous verses, but it is actually upon all who have embraced apostasy. Why? Because men were originally created with the power of choice. They live as they do because of the choices they make. The men in the past chose to sin. They were not predestined by some sadistic god to follow that route. They were not powerless individuals compelled by some inborn force.

Before Cain ever killed Abel, God was faithful to him and spoke to him. He confronted Cain with a choice. Genesis 4:6-7 states: “And the L ORD said unto Cain, Why art thou wroth? and why is thy countenance fallen? If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door.”

Genesis 1:27 says that God created man in his own image. Colossians 3:10 tells us, “the new man . . . is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him.” Ephesians 4:24 says, “Put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness.” So to be in God’s image, you must be living morally right and without sin.

God created Adam and Eve in His likeness, in righteousness and holiness, and every other person who has been born into this world has been born in the same sin-free state. Ecclesiastes 7:29 substantiates this: “Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright.” Ezekiel 28:15 says, “Thou wast perfect in thy ways from the day that thou wast created, till iniquity was found in thee.” When does man lose his perfection? Man remains perfect until he willingly chooses to go contrary to the known will of God.

Why does man turn to his own way and go astray? Is the environment the cause? Is some supposed inherited sin or Adamic nature to blame? No. We go astray and sin in how we exercise our power of choice. Throughout the Scriptures, men have been divinely advised to make the right choice. Apostates do not want to accept the fact that their condition is the result of a wrong choice. They want to blame their pastor, the congregation, their husbands, their wives, or others. However, the truth is, they have chosen to be there. Refusing to Obey Truth

In the way of Cain. Cain holds two unique places in Bible history: he was the first child to be born, and he committed the first murder. The account of that murder in Genesis 4:2-5 reads: “Abel was a keeper of sheep, but Cain was a tiller of the ground. And in process of time it came to pass, that Cain brought of the fruit of the ground an offering unto the L ORD . And Abel, he also brought of the firstlings of his flock and of the fat thereof. And the L ORD had respect unto Abel and to his offering: But unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect.”

Many suppositions have been made as to why God accepted one offering and rejected the other. Some say Cain should have taken his fruit and traded it for a sheep to offer as an acceptable sacrifice–but this was many years before the Law was given. Why then, was a distinction made between the offerings? Exodus 23:19 says, “The first of the firstfruits of thy land thou shalt bring into the house of the L ORD thy God.” Abel brought the “firstlings of his flock” to God, but Cain brought his offering from the earth “in process of time.” Cain was not devout or diligent.

In Genesis 4:6 the Lord asked Cain why he was angry. What produced his wrath? Religious jealousy. Abel’s offering was accepted but Cain’s was not. Why not? Sin was at his door, according to Genesis 4:7. It was ready to spring and devour him. The Lord had warned Cain that if he stepped outside the bounds of what he knew was right, sin would be crouching, waiting to pounce on him, and he would be at its mercy. When he refused to dwell in the truth God had shown him, he became true to his name, which means “possessed.” He rose up against Abel (which means “breath or vapor”) and killed him.
The Tongue–A Weapon

What was Jude trying to tell us about ones who have gone in the way of Cain? Just this: they, as Cain, want to worship God in their own manner, at their own convenience, and contrary to truth. Ones who are righteous bring condemnation to apostates, and just as Cain did, apostates murder them. 1 John 3:15 proclaims, “Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him.”

In what manner do apostates murder their righteous brothers? Jeremiah 18:18 has the answer: “Come, and let us smite him with the tongue, and let us not give heed to any of his words.” Apostates go in the way of Cain when they slander the righteous ones and attempt to kill their influence. 1 John 3:11-12 says: “We should love one another. Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother. . . . Because his own works were evil, and his brother’s righteous.”

Those whose works are contrary to truth and love would like to stomp out truth with their murderous tongues; but 2 Corinthians 13:8 declares, “We can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth.” Regardless of the apostates’ intention to destroy the saints and the church, the Church of God has endured numerous assaults throughout history. It will continue to endure them because Jesus said in Matthew 16:18, “I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.”
JUST A THOUGHT
Did it ever occur to you that nothing ever occurs to God?

LESSON 11
THE ERROR OF BALAAM–PART 1
Scripture Text: Jude 11

In this lesson, we will begin to study the second Old Testament character in verse 11: Balaam. This character study has been divided into two parts because the error of Balaam has at least two major aspects to it. We will learn that he committed an act that Jude used to show the sad condition of apostates.
MEMORY VERSE: And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth. ─Luke 12:15
Balak Summons Balaam

Balaam. What relation did Balaam have to Jude’s day and even to our day? We must know what occurred historically to understand the reasons Jude referred to him. Israel entered Canaan in B.C.1451, but as they were nearing the end of forty years of wandering in the wilderness, they met the elders of Moab and Midian, who feared what Israel might do to them (see Numbers, Chapters 22-24).

Balak, the king of the Moabites, had seen all that the Israelites had done to the Amorites. He sent messengers to Balaam (the name means “destruction of the people”) saying, “Come now therefore, I pray thee, curse me this people . . . for I wot [know] that he whom thou blessest is blessed, and he whom thou cursest is cursed” (Numbers 22:6).
One Aspect of the Error

The error of Balaam. When Balak’s representatives came and presented their request to Balaam, he initially said the right thing. Numbers 22:8 reads, “Lodge here this night, and I will bring you word again, as the L ORD shall speak unto me.” He started out right because, before he made any decision or commitment, he prayed. God told him, “Thou shalt not go with them; thou shalt not curse the people: for they are blessed” (Numbers 22:12). After praying, Balaam told the men that the Lord refused to give him leave to go with them. That should have been the end of it! However, Balak sent more princes who offered Balaam more honor and riches; then, he committed the first aspect of his error.

The Greek word for error is the word plane, meaning “a wandering, a forsaking of the right path.” Balaam had already prayed, and he knew the will of God, but he said, “Tarry ye also here this night, that I may know what the L ORD will say unto me more” (Numbers 22:19). This was the fatal part of the error: he prayed again hoping for a different answer to the same question. This is always a grave mistake! Malachi 3:6 states, “For I am the L ORD , I change not,” and Psalm 119:89 says, “Forever, O L ORD , thy word is settled in heaven.”

The erring, or the “forsaking” of the right way, comes when one knows to do good but does not do it, then to him it becomes sin (James 4:17). Balaam knew what was the good and right thing to do, but he left what he knew was spiritually right to willingly follow what his flesh craved. Even so, God was as faithful to him.
Running for Reward

Ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward. One translation of this phrase says that they “abandon themselves for the sake of gain.” Another translation says, “For the sake of gain they have rushed on headlong.” Each translation shows the sad reality that once a person has forsaken the truth, the restraint of God’s grace is not there anymore. The flesh takes hold of the individual with a dominant control, and that person rushes to fulfill fleshly desires.

LESSON 11

What would prompt people to do as Balaam did? 2 Peter 2:14-15 says: “. . . an heart they have exercised with covetous practices; cursed children: Which have forsaken the right way, and are gone astray, following the way of Balaam . . . who loved the wages of unrighteousness.” In verse 16 Peter called the Prophet’s actions “madness.” Certainly, ones are mad to forfeit eternal reward for temporal gain.
Conditions of Today

In Jude and Peter’s day, people who had known the truth and been established in it were being duped by a spirit that appealed to the flesh. 2 Peter 2:20 says, “For if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled therein, and overcome, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning.”

In this day, we are having an evening-time apostasy much like that of the morning time. Many have been able to get hold of God, hear from God, and take a clear stand on revealed truth; but over time, something has happened. Just as Balaam was offered great honor and riches, the enemy has his agents who are trying to lure the saints away from truth. They appeal to your sense of reason and make it seem reasonable for you to forsake truth. You must be watchful that seducing spirits do not cause you to follow the flesh.

Many people today determine the stand they will take or the moves they will make by first deciding which will gain them the greatest reward or be the most favorable for their flesh. They suppose “that gain is godliness . . . . But godliness with contentment is great gain” (1 Timothy 6:5-6).

Haggai 1:6 says, “He that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes.” The more you put into “a bag with holes,” the more it needs. This is exactly the way the flesh is. Once you begin to cater to it, you can never satisfy it. You will only turn from fulfillment to frustration and become enslaved by trying to satisfy fleshly passions and desires.
JUST A THOUGHT
When you hear something about a brother, go to the throne instead of the phone.

LESSON 12
THE ERROR OF BALAAM–PART 2
Scripture Text: Jude 11

As we review the text, we can see that each character so far has been involved in religious activity. This clearly disproves the thought of, “If it is religious, then it must be good.” Throughout history many things were done by numerous individuals in the name of religion, but that certainly did not mean that they were right or that what they did was based in the truth.

In the previous lesson, one part of the error of Balaam was that he prayed about whether to go with Balak’s princes when he already knew the will of God. In this lesson, when Balaam could not curse Israel, he conceived something worse with results that were more terrible and disastrous. This second episode is what left its mark on Hebrew thought and teaching.
MEMORY VERSE: Who knowing the judgment of God, that they which commit such things are worthy of death, not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them. ─Romans 1:32
Balaam’s Ungodly Counsel

Psalm 1:1 states, “Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly.” When Balaam saw that he could not curse what God had blessed, he advised the women of Midian and Moab to seduce the Israelite men and cause them to sin. He did this for reward. (The moves that were made in the morning time and the ones being made today have come about from fleshly, carnal reasons and for temporal rewards, rather than from divine guidance.) Balaam reasoned that if the Israelites would sin, then the Lord would have to punish them, Balak’s purpose would be served, and he, Balaam, would be rich. Numbers 25:1-2 relates the result of that plan: “And Israel abode in Shittim, and the people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab. And they called the people . . . and the people did eat, and bowed down to their gods.”

Three lessons can be learned from these verses. First, ungodly counsel affects not only the ones who receive it but also those they have influence over. Second, close relationships can cause us to do something that we normally would not do. Third, our affiliations with those whose worship and religion is different from the truth can pull us into falsity.
A Spiritual Seduction

In Revelation 2:14, Jesus spoke of “the doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balac to cast a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat things sacrificed unto idols, and to commit fornication.” Why did Jude bring up the thought of seduction in connection with apostasy? Because, just as seducers had worked under the council of Balaam, there were spiritual seducers working in the first century.

Balaam used women to tempt Israel’s men to commit literal fornication. Satan uses seducing spirits to tempt the saints to commit spiritual fornication. 1 Corinthians 6:18 admonishes us to “flee fornication.” Those who took on seducing spirits in Jude’s day and left the truth and the true church but continued to profess to belong to Christ were, in reality, engaging in spiritual fornication.
The Goal of Satan

Numbers 25:2 says that “the people did eat, and bowed down to their gods.” Here the enemies’ original intent is seen. It was to get the Israelites to come down to the level of worshiping “their gods.” This is the true motive of apostates. They will woo you, love you, and show you much kindness; just as Solomon’s strange

wives did to him. They won his heart first; then they “turned away his heart after other gods” (1 Kings 11:4).
Friend, the enemy’s ultimate goal is your heart! Satan wants to use anyone with a seducing spirit to tempt you so that you will turn to a false system of worship.

Joshua 13:22 says that Balaam was slain “with the sword.” His end was physical death. The end of apostasy is spiritual death. Today’s idols may not be of stone, of gold, or of silver. They are more deceptive and damning. Your only defense is the truth. You should love it, obey it, and not deviate from it. LESSON 13
THE GAINSAYING OF CORE
Scripture Text: Jude 11

This lesson focuses on Core. His Hebrew name was Korah, which we are more familiar with. He was the last of the three men, in this verse, to serve as an example of the sad fate of apostates. We should not overlook the fact that all the statements in Jude 11 are in the past tense. In God’s sight, those who have been overcome by an apostate spirit have already perished. Romans 4:17 says that God “calleth those things which be not as though they were.” The fate of apostates is just as certain as the glorification of the saints.
Memory Verse: But shun profane and vain babblings: for they will increase unto more ungodliness. ─2 Timothy 2:16
Who Was Core?

Why did Jude use Core? He was a Levite and a cousin to Moses (see Exodus 6:18-21). He had great influence in the congregation. Along with two others, he started an insurrection, a rebellion, against Moses’ authority. Numbers 16:2 says that “they rose up before Moses, with certain of the children of Israel, two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, famous in the congregation, men of renown.” This verse teaches that men who are highly revered and have tremendous influence, such as those in positions, are the ones the enemy would like to use to work against the cause of God. Then, it teaches that you ought to be extremely cautious about what you lend your influence and your name to.
The One Mediator

Numbers 16:3 says that Core charged Moses, saying, “Ye take too much upon you . . . wherefore then lift ye up yourselves above the congregation of the L ORD ?” It is easy to see that religious jealousy was at the root of this rebellion. Proverbs 6:34 says, “Jealousy is the rage of a man.” When one is overtaken by jealousy, he becomes enraged, cruel, and does not exercise proper restraint.

Core rose up against Moses’ authority and God’s divine plan. Moses was a type of Christ; Aaron was a type of the ministry. When those men opposed Moses and Aaron, they were in direct rebellion to God’s plan for a mediator. 1 Timothy 2:5 states, “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.” They thought (as religion thinks today) that there could be many avenues, or mediators, but God had chosen just one: Moses. In our day, Jesus Christ is our mediator–Mary cannot intercede for us and neither can a priest or a preacher–only Christ!
Perishing in Apostasy

Perished in the gainsaying of Core. The word gainsaying comes from the Greek word antilogia. Anti means “against”; logia means “the word.” Combined, they mean “against the word.” By studying verse 11, we can see how apostasy worsens. Cain “ignored” the Word that had been spoken to him personally. Balaam “subtly opposed” the Word that had been revealed to him. Core “openly rebelled” against the Word of God. His name means “ice cold,” and he stood in cold-hearted defiance against God’s plan, God’s man, and God’s Word– and he was punished for his actions.

How did he perish? Moses told him to gather all his men before God at the door of the tabernacle. What happened? “There came out a fire from the L ORD , and consumed the two hundred and fifty men that offered

incense” (Numbers 16:35). This is another type. Hebrews 12:29 says that God is a consuming fire. What is it about God that is a fire? “Is not my word like as a fire?” (Jeremiah 23:29). What is the lesson here for us? Those who are not on fire for God will be burned by the fire of God. The same Word we refuse and rebel against will put judgment on us.
Taking a Stand

Throughout the Psalms there are songs that have the caption: “To the chief Musician for the sons of Korah.” What is the significance of this? Core took a very rebellious stance toward the Word and perished for it; but when his sons were confronted with a choice, they obeyed the man of God and even stood against their father. God honored their stand, and they became the most renowned temple singers in David’s day. Friend, you may be required to stand against those you love the dearest to avoid being drawn into apostasy, but your love and allegiance to the truth must be supreme.
JUST A THOUGHT
To avoid repeating history, one must know it!

LESSON 1
AN INTRODUCTION TO THE EPISTLE OF JUDE
Scripture Text: Jude 1-2
The Epistle of Jude has been placed in the New Testament as a gateway to The
Revelation. It is richer in symbolic language than any other book in the New Testament
with the exception of The Revelation. The Acts of the Apostles clearly shows the acts of
the “Apostles,” but the Epistle of Jude reveals the acts of the “apostates.” In this evening
time of the Gospel Day, we are again facing the forces of apostasy. Jude has provided us
with insight and revelation concerning the spirits that are promoting apostasy, the
behavior that it produces, and how the enemy intends to work through apostasy today.
MEMORY VERSE: Is there any thing whereof it may be said, See, this is new? it hath been already of old
time, which was before us (Ecclesiastes 1:10).
Jude, the Author
Jude, the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James. In the original Greek, the name Jude is actually
Judas. The very title of this book brings to mind the person who will stand forever known as the world’s best
example of the worst apostate–Judas Iscariot! In the New Testament, five notable men were called Judas, but
this man is clearly identified as the brother of James. James was the pastor of the Jerusalem congregation, the
author of the Epistle of James, and one of the four brothers of the Lord (Matthew 13:55).
Preventions of Apostasy
Attributes portrayed by both Jude and James can prevent one’s being infected with apostasy. One attribute is
humility. Notice, Jude did not mention the fact that he was the Lord’s brother. This shows the lack of carnal
pride. Proverbs 13:10 states, “Only by pride cometh contention.” Unfeigned humility causes one “not to think
of himself more highly than he ought to think” (Romans 12:3).
Another attribute is servitude. Both Jude and James stated that they were servants. The English word servant
is the word doulos in the original Greek and means much more than a servant. It means “a slave,” or literally, “a
bondslave.”
The greatest prevention of our apostatizing or backsliding is to be continually aware that we are the Church
of God. We have been purchased with Jesus Christ’s blood (Acts 20:28). We should glorify God in our bodies
and in our spirits, which are God’s. One who is truly a slave to the Master and His Word will never apostatize.
The Audience Addressed by Jude
To them that are sanctified by God the Father, and preserved in Jesus Christ, and called. The word
called is derived from the Greek word kalein, which means “the summoning of a man to office, to duty, and to
responsibility.” It represents the saints’ call to arms. They are to be watchful for the most subtle moves of the
enemy. The word sanctified comes from the Greek word hagiazo and means “the setting apart of the believer for
God.” We must be set apart and totally yielded to God with self kept under to maintain victory over apostasy.
The word preserved comes from a Greek word that means “kept,” or “continually kept.” It expresses
watchful care and close attention. The Apostle Paul referred to his readers as sanctified and called, but Jude
added preserved to show, right in verse one, that no matter how great the opposing force may be, Christ has
made provision for His people to be “continually kept.”

LESSON 1
Mercy, Peace, and Love
Mercy unto you, and peace, and love, be multiplied. This second verse is more than a courteous
salutation; it is the only such statement in the entire Bible. The Apostle Paul used the phrase “grace be unto you,
and peace” in Colossians 1:2, but Jude used the word Mercy, meaning “an outward manifestation of pity.” It
assumes there is a need on the part of the person who receives it and reveals describes man’s upward look to
God. Peace depicts man’s inward look at what God gives. Love radiates from man’s heart through his outward
look. These verses describe the qualities the church needs to maintain constant victory in these troublesome
times.

Hate is a small word with big consequences.

LESSON 2
JUDE’S BURDEN
Scripture Text: Jude 3
This lesson reveals the burden behind Jude’s letter. Jude was in the process of
drafting a doctrinal treatise but set it hastily aside when necessity and inspiration
prompted him, because his divinely inspired burden compelled him to write. In our
day, when many make a professional vocation out of religion, the true church still
looks for those who have been divinely called and have a burden prompting them in
what they do.
MEMORY VERSE: For though I preach the gospel, I have nothing to glory of:
for necessity is laid upon me; yea, woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel (1
Corinthians 9:16)!
Letter to the Church
Beloved. Jude addressed his readers as Beloved. He was speaking to those whom God loves, those who have
been born again. They are the ones who can understand spiritual truth. 1 Corinthians 2:14 reads, “But the
natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know
them, because they are spiritually discerned.”
The Greek word for beloved is agapetos. It is derived from another Greek word, agapao, which stands for
divine love, a never changing love. Jude wrote this letter to the church–a people whose true love for Christ and
truth is unchanging, even in changing times.
The Common Salvation
When I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation. Another translation of this phrase
reads, “When I was in the midst of devoting all my energy to writing to you about the faith we all share.” Both
phrases teach that we will each have the same salvation: it will work in the same manner in all.
The word common comes from the Greek word koinos and means “shared by all.” Concerning doctrinal
truths and standards, the common salvation will not lead some people in one direction and others in a contrary
direction. If that is occurring, something other than real salvation is working. Ones may claim it is salvation, but
if it is not common, it is not real.
Unchangeable Word of Truth
Exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
Jude wrote this epistle in A.D. 66, only thirty-three years after the Day of Pentecost. His real reason for writing
was to reveal that an apostasy was already under way. That which was being presented to the people as salvation
and Christianity was not really the faith but a cleverly disguised counterfeit.
The words contend for the faith . . . once delivered unto the saints hold several truths. One, the faith is
delivered. Truth is not some “vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers” (1 Peter 1:18). It is not
something that comes by education but by revelation. Peter spoke concerning prophecy, but this principle is true
of all Scriptures: “Holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2 Peter 1:21). The Apostle
Paul said, “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2 Timothy 3:16).
Two, the faith has an unchangeable quality. Though man may present other things and try to pass them off as
Christianity, true faith never changes; it is based in the divine. Jesus said in John 14:6, “I am the way, the truth,
and the life.” Hebrews 13:8 says that “Jesus Christ [is] the same yesterday, and today, and forever,” and

Malachi 3:6 says, “For I am the L ORD , I change not.” Since the Source of Truth is unchanging and settled, so is
His truth. Psalm 119:89 states, “Forever, O L ORD , thy word is settled in heaven.” The faith is still what mankind
needs today.
Three, truths was given to saints. Notice, the word is saints (plural). Truth is not the possession of any one
individual: it comes down within the church, it is understood by the church, and the church is responsible to
propagate it.
Four, truth must be defended. In the text, the word contend actually means “to defend.” Bagster’s Greek
Lexicon says this word means “to contend strenuously in defense of.” The word Jude used contains the root of
our English word agony. Defending the Word, or the truth, may not always be easy or comfortable: it may cause
some agony. In this day of ease, many do not want to be inconvenienced, but in order to preserve the truth and
defend the faith, we may suffer much discomfort. However, it is better to be uncomfortable here for a season
than for all eternity.
JUST A THOUGHT
Some are contenders; others are pretenders.

LESSON 3
EARMARKS OF APOSTATES
Scripture Text: Jude 4
In this lesson, Jude exposed the earmarks of the apostate elements that were working.
This epistle and others have been preserved down through the years to help us understand
these conditions when we see them developing. Jude has shown us that the only way to
deal with apostasy is with truth. Truth is plain and pointed; it exposes wrong.
Ephesians 6:12 says, “For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against
principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against
spiritual wickedness [or wicked spirits] in high places [another text says „heavenlies‟].” In
today‟s society when one raises his voice against wrong or apostasy, he is quickly branded as having a bad
spirit. In the light of our text, the one who promotes a teaching, a doctrine, or a stance contrary to the sound
teaching of the Scriptures is the one with a bad spirit.
MEMORY VERSE: For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, Teaching us
that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present
world (Titus 2:11-12).
Workers of Deceit
There are certain men crept in unawares. Here is the peril that prompted Jude to write this flaming epistle.
Why such alarm? The danger to the church was coming from within! Men who were not actually in the church–
the body of Christ–were being accepted as brethren in the congregation, making their influence and teachings
dangerous.
In the original Greek language, the word pareisduein is used for the words crept in unawares. It describes the
slow and subtle entry of new ways or ideas that seek to undermine and break down traditional values. It always
indicates something evil coming into a society or a situation. This word represents a clever pleader who–by his
logic, his argument, and his persuasive personality–wins the minds of a judge and jury. It is also used to portray
an outlaw slipping back into a country from which he had been deported. Jude 4 in The Amplified Bible reads,
“For certain men have crept in stealthily [gaining entrance secretly by a side door].” John 10:1 states, “He that
entereth not by the door [Jesus] . . . the same is a thief and a robber.”
Jesus spoke of apostasy in Matthew 13:25 when he said, “But while men slept, his enemy came and sowed
tares among the wheat.” The enemy‟s introduction of deceitful men into the Christian community was as
disastrous as tares being sown into a crop of wheat. Tares entwine their roots around wheat and when they are
removed, the wheat is ripped up as well. This is how deadly it can be when people like that work in a
congregation if the “wheat” is not truly “rooted and grounded” (Ephesians 3:17). Matthew 15:13 says, “Every
plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up.” So, the first earmark of apostates is that
these people work slowly and undercover. If they were dealing truthfully, they would not have to work in such
an underhanded manner.
Perverting God’s Grace
Ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness. The second earmark of a move made by
an apostate is that it leans toward less godliness. It lowers the standard of holiness and makes provision for the
flesh. This is always a sure indicator of apostasy!
Apostates do not outwardly appear to be ungodly men (this is a general term that includes women as well).
This term is derived from the Greek word abebes, which means “one destitute of reverential awe toward God.”
The reason these ones can accomplish such a deceptive work is that they do not tremble at God‟s Word! Jesus

said they are “like unto whited sepulchres” that “outwardly appear righteous unto men” (Matthew 23:27-28).
Concerning externals, these people are blameless, but “within they are full of extortion and excess” (verse
25). The Amplified Bible is more graphic: “Within they are full of extortion (prey, spoil, plunder) and grasping
self-indulgence.”
The men who lacked the fear of God in Jude‟s day took hold of that which was divine and began to alter it,
over a period of time, to suit their own fleshly purposes. Through persistence, they began turning the grace (the
strength, or power) of our God into lasciviousness (blatant immorality).
In the first century there were two groups of people known as the Antinomians and the Gnostics. These
individuals embraced lawlessness. They taught that matter was wholly evil; therefore, the body being matter was
evil–so man could not live holy–but the grace of God would cover any sin. This meant that man could sin as
much as he wanted, because the more he sinned, the greater the grace. The Bible‟s response to such a teaching
is, “Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid” (Romans 6:1-2).
Denying the Lord
Denying the only Lord God, and our Lord Jesus Christ. The third earmark of apostates is denial. When
the thought of denying the only Lord God is raised, people think it means to actually deny that He exists, but this
is not what the Scripture text implies. How do ones deny God? Titus 1:16 tells us that they profess to know
Him; but really, in works they deny Him. The Amplified Bible says, “They profess to know God [to recognize,
perceive and be acquainted with Him] but deny and disown and renounce Him by what they do.”
Christ is referred to as our Lord Jesus Christ. This phrase portrays the three offices of Christ. One, He is
Sovereign of the universe and “Lord of all” (Acts 10:36). Two, He is Jesus, which means “Jehovah the Savior.”
Three, He is Christ, or Christos, in Greek and Messiah in Hebrew, which means “The Anointed One,” the
fulfillment of Old Testament prophecy.
The apostates in Jude‟s day denied Christ lordship of their lives, refused His salvation and deliverance, and
discarded Him as “The Anointed One.” They denied Him in works and substituted another gospel for the truth
(Galatians 1:6). However, God is faithful. He has had a ministry to sound forth an alarm in every age of time.
Whether we heed it or not in our day will determine our outcome.
JUST A THOUGHT
Failure may be an event; it need not be a person.
